patient.name: Doreen Pemberton
patient.setting: Emergency Department (sent in from her care home)
patient.complaint: Three days of diarrhoea, drinking very little, now dizzy and muddled
background: Norovirus outbreak at her care home in Lewisham
Mild memory problems; usually chatty and independent with a frame
Baseline creatinine 80 µmol/L three months ago

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely finding' with an older or unwell patient losing fluid (vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperglycaemia) plus dry mucous membranes, tachycardia and a urea that has risen far more than the creatinine.

points: Doreen, 84, has had **watery diarrhoea for 3 days**.
Carers say she has barely drunk anything.
Today she felt **dizzy on standing** and is muddled.
She has passed very little dark urine since yesterday.

steps.lead: Doreen has lost more water than she has taken in: a **body water deficit** that has shrunk her circulating volume.
Her cause is **diarrhoea plus poor intake**. In a diabetic with polyuria, think osmotic diuresis instead.

points: Skin on her hand tents and returns slowly (**reduced turgor**).
JVP not visible lying flat; capillary refill 4 seconds.

steps.lead: Doreen's **hypotension and confusion** put her in the **severe** group, not the thirsty, dry-mouthed mild group.

steps.q: Which finding most clearly tells you Doreen's dehydration is severe?
steps.r: **Hypotension and confusion** mean organ perfusion is failing: severe dehydration. The others occur in mild to moderate cases too.

steps.lead: Doreen's bloods (next) show the signature: **urea up far more than creatinine**, with a high sodium and haematocrit.
Her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 80: she is developing **pre-renal AKI**, made worse by her ramipril and thiazide.

steps.text: In older people, **thirst is blunted** and skin turgor is unreliable. Lean on the pulse, BP, urine output and bloods, not on whether she says she is thirsty.

investigation.exam: Dehydration is a **clinical** diagnosis. Questions test that U&Es come first, that **urea** is the most sensitive marker, and that the urine is concentrated (high osmolality), unlike diabetes insipidus.

steps.lead: Doreen's diagnosis is already made at the bedside from her history, pulse, BP and dry mucous membranes. Tests measure the damage.

steps.title: Doreen's bloods
steps.text: Urea is 2.5 times the upper limit; creatinine much less so. High sodium and haematocrit: the blood is concentrated.

steps.lead: Doreen's **U&Es** are the key first test: urea is the most sensitive marker, and her sodium and creatinine are raised too.

visual.title: Urea:creatinine ratio (urea ÷ creatinine × 1000)
visual.label: Doreen 138
visual.caption: 19.6 ÷ 142 × 1000 = **138**. A ratio above about 100 points to a pre-renal, dry state rather than intrinsic kidney damage.

steps.q: Doreen's urea is 19.6 and creatinine 142. What does the disproportionate urea rise suggest?
steps.r: Urea rising **far more** than creatinine is the classic marker of a **pre-renal**, volume-depleted state.

steps.lead: Doreen's urine is dark and concentrated (osmolality 810 mOsm/kg). Glucose and FBC rule out hyperglycaemia and show the high haematocrit.

steps.text: An upper GI bleed also raises urea out of proportion (digested blood protein), but the **haemoglobin falls**. In dehydration the haematocrit **rises**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': decide mild-moderate (**oral rehydration solution**) versus severe (**IV 0.9% saline**). Burns that fail crystalloid get human albumin solution. Correct sodium slowly.

steps.lead: First grade Doreen's severity. A thirsty, alert resident with normal BP would get **ORS** by mouth.

steps.q: Doreen is hypotensive, tachycardic and confused. What is the most appropriate initial fluid?
steps.r: Severe dehydration with hypotension needs **IV 0.9% saline**. 5% glucose does not stay in the circulation; she is too unwell for oral fluid.

steps.lead: Doreen gets a **0.9% saline** bolus, then reassessment of pulse, BP and urine output.

steps.title: Rehydration pathway
nodes: Assess: history, pulse, BP, mental state, urine output
Mild to moderate → oral rehydration solution
steps.caption: Severity decides the route; the U&Es decide the pace.

steps.lead: Doreen's sodium of 151 is brought down **slowly**, her low potassium replaced, and her diarrhoea managed. Her ramipril and thiazide are held.

visual.title: Doreen's first 48 hours
visual.caption: Sodium falls by about **8 mmol/L in 24 hours**, not all at once, as her urine output and urea recover.

steps.lead: Doreen has no burns, but remember: in **severe burns** where crystalloid alone fails, **human albumin solution** restores intravascular volume.
Doreen's fluids follow the **NICE IV fluid guidance**: assess, resuscitate with a crystalloid bolus, reassess, then replace ongoing losses.

steps.text: Do not 'fix' a sodium of 151 in a few hours. **Rapid correction** of hypernatraemic dehydration risks **cerebral oedema** and seizures.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why the urine is concentrated (RAAS and ADH), why urea rises more than creatinine, and why fast correction of hypernatraemia causes cerebral oedema.

steps.lead: Doreen's diarrhoea lost water and salt, but she lost **more water**, so her dehydration is **hypertonic** (sodium 151).
Doreen's low volume switches on **RAAS and ADH**, so her kidneys hold on to water and sodium: small amounts of dark urine.

steps.title: Why the urine gets concentrated
nodes: Renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone: sodium kept
ADH released → aquaporins in collecting duct

steps.lead: As Doreen's tubules pull back water, **urea follows passively**; creatinine does not, so her urea climbs much faster.
Doreen's BP of 92/58 shows she is sliding towards **hypovolaemic shock**; her brain cells have adapted to the high sodium, so correction must be slow.

visual.title: Fall in sodium over 24 hours
visual.label: Doreen 8
visual.caption: Doreen's sodium fell 8 mmol/L in the first day. Faster than about 10 to 12 mmol/L a day lets water rush into adapted brain cells.

steps.text: Opposite directions, different brain risks: correcting **high** sodium too fast causes **cerebral oedema**; correcting **low** sodium too fast causes **osmotic demyelination**.

mcq.r: A **deficit of body water**, reducing circulating volume and upsetting electrolytes.

mcq.q: Which is a feature of severe rather than mild dehydration?
mcq.r: **Hypotension**, confusion and shock mark severe dehydration.

mcq.q: Which blood pattern is the classic signature of dehydration?
o: Raised urea out of proportion to creatinine
mcq.r: A **disproportionate urea rise**, with hypernatraemia and a high haematocrit.

mcq.q: Which renal complication does dehydration cause?
What is the most sensitive blood marker of dehydration?
What urine finding is expected in dehydration?
mcq.r: **Concentrated urine with high osmolality**. Dilute urine with high sodium suggests diabetes insipidus.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration?
What is the treatment of severe dehydration?
mcq.r: **IV 0.9% saline**. HAS is for severe burns when crystalloid alone fails.

mcq.q: Why does overly rapid correction of hypernatraemic dehydration cause cerebral oedema?
o: Adapted brain cells take up water too quickly
Sodium crystals deposit in the brain
The brain loses water too quickly
mcq.r: Brain cells adapted to a **hypertonic** environment take up water too fast.

mcq.q: Which hormones concentrate the urine in dehydration?
mcq.r: Low volume activates **RAAS** and **ADH**, increasing water and sodium reabsorption.

technique.stem: An 81 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department from his care home. He has had diarrhoea for 4 days and has been drinking very little. He is drowsy. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. His mucous membranes are dry and his JVP is not visible. Urine output is low.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with U&Es: look at the pattern and the urine.
Fluid loss with poor intake, tachycardia, hypotension, dry and flat JVP. Urea up far more than creatinine; concentrated urine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe **dehydration** with pre-renal AKI.

elim: Addison's gives low sodium and high potassium; his sodium is high.
DI gives large volumes of dilute urine; his urine is scanty and concentrated.
No calcium given, and the history is clear fluid loss.
SIADH causes low sodium in a euvolaemic patient.

steps.x: **B. Dehydration.** Rule: fluid loss + high urea:creatinine + concentrated urine = dehydration.

technique.stem: A 76 year old woman has had vomiting for 2 days and feels dizzy on standing. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg lying, falling on standing. Her mouth is dry. Blood tests are sent.
technique.q: Which result is the most sensitive marker of her dehydration?

steps.x: Asks which marker is the most sensitive, not which is abnormal.
Clinically dry. Urea has doubled; creatinine has barely moved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urea** is the most sensitive marker.

elim: Albumin is normal and is not a sensitive marker here.
Creatinine rises later and less, since it is not reabsorbed with water.
Potassium is normal and varies with the type of loss.
Sodium is raised but less consistently; it depends on the type of fluid lost.

steps.x: **E. Urea.** Rule: urea is the most sensitive U&E marker of dehydration.

technique.stem: An 88 year old woman with dementia is admitted after a week of poor oral intake. She is given intravenous fluids. Her pulse rate is now 88 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Her serum sodium on admission is 156 mmol/L (135–145). The junior doctor plans to bring it back to normal by this evening.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to correcting her sodium?
o: Correct the sodium to normal within 6 hours
Lower the sodium slowly with regular monitoring

steps.x: A management question about the speed of sodium correction.

clues: back to normal by this evening
steps.x: Chronic hypernatraemic dehydration: the brain has adapted.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Correct **slowly**, monitoring sodium and potassium, to avoid cerebral oedema.

elim: Fast correction risks cerebral oedema and seizures.
Hypertonic saline raises sodium further.
Furosemide removes more water; she is dry.
Restricting fluid worsens a water deficit.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: correct electrolytes slowly and monitor; treat the cause.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man is admitted with severe dehydration and a serum sodium of 158 mmol/L after a week of poor intake. He is given large volumes of intravenous 5% glucose. Twelve hours later his sodium is 141 mmol/L. He becomes drowsy and has a generalised seizure. His capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?

steps.x: A mechanism question: what happened to the brain after fluids.

clues: Twelve hours later his sodium is 141 mmol/L
steps.x: Sodium fell by 17 mmol/L in 12 hours: far too fast for adapted brain cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cerebral oedema**: brain cells adapted to a hypertonic state took up water too quickly.

elim: Nothing suggests low calcium.
Glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
No trauma, anticoagulant or focal signs; the timing fits the fast sodium fall.
Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction of LOW sodium.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: high sodium corrected fast = cerebral oedema; low sodium corrected fast = demyelination.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman is brought in by her daughter after 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. She is lethargic and has hardly passed urine. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Her tongue is dry and skin turgor is reduced.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fluid losses, tachycardia, hypotension, dry tongue and a disproportionate urea rise with concentrated urine mean dehydration. DI gives dilute urine.

steps.x: Diagnosis with U&Es and urine osmolality.
Losses, oliguria, tachycardia, low BP, dry. Urea up far more than creatinine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dehydration**.

elim: ATN gives a proportionate rise and dilute, salty urine.
DI gives large volumes of dilute urine.
Nephrotic syndrome gives oedema and proteinuria, not dryness.
SIADH gives low sodium in a euvolaemic patient.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: concentrated urine plus high urea:creatinine = dehydration.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man returns from a festival with 2 days of profuse watery diarrhoea. He feels thirsty and lightheaded. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The doctor suspects he is dehydrated and examines him.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Dehydration causes dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor. The other options are signs of fluid overload.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding in dehydration.
Fluid loss with thirst and tachycardia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dry mucous membranes**.

elim: Crackles suggest fluid overload or infection.
A bounding pulse fits CO2 retention or sepsis; dehydration gives a weak, fast pulse.
Oedema means fluid overload.
A raised JVP means fluid overload; his would be low.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: dry, not overloaded: dry mucosa, low JVP, poor turgor.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has had gastroenteritis for 3 days. He is drinking small amounts of water. The doctor is deciding whether his dehydration is mild to moderate or severe.
practice.q: Which finding would most indicate severe dehydration?
practice.e: Severe dehydration shows hypotension, confusion, tachycardia and shock. Thirst and dry mouth occur in mild to moderate dehydration.

steps.x: A severity question: which sign means severe.
You need the sign of failing perfusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypotension and confusion**.

elim: Dry mouth occurs in mild to moderate dehydration.
Fatigue is non-specific and seen in mild cases.
Thirst is a mild to moderate feature.
Reduced appetite does not grade severity.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: hypotension, confusion or shock = severe = IV fluids.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has a week of thirst and passing large volumes of urine. She is now dizzy. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. She has no vomiting or diarrhoea and has been drinking more than usual.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her dehydration?
practice.e: Glucose spills into the urine and drags water with it: an osmotic diuresis. Her intake is up, not down, and DI does not cause hyperglycaemia.

steps.x: Asks the cause of the dehydration.
Glucose 29 with glycosuria and polyuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osmotic diuresis** from hyperglycaemia.

elim: Addison's gives low sodium, high potassium and hypoglycaemia, not glucose 29.
DI causes polyuria without hyperglycaemia or glycosuria.
No history of heat or exercise.
She is drinking more than usual.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: diabetes dehydrates through osmotic diuresis.

practice.stem: An 83 year old man on ramipril has had diarrhoea for 5 days. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 90/58 mmHg. He has passed 150 mL of urine in 12 hours. His creatinine three months ago was 85 µmol/L. A bladder scan shows 40 mL residual urine.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised creatinine?
practice.e: Dehydration reduces kidney perfusion, causing pre-renal AKI; the disproportionate urea rise and clean dipstick fit. Normal CK excludes rhabdomyolysis; small residual excludes obstruction.

steps.x: The cause of a creatinine rise: a complication question.
Dehydration, hypotension, ACE inhibitor, oliguria; no retention. Urea:creatinine is about 137.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pre-renal AKI** from dehydration.

elim: AIN follows a new drug, often with rash and eosinophilia.
GN gives blood and protein on dipstick; it is clean.
Only 40 mL residual: no obstruction.
CK is normal.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: dehydration's key renal complication is pre-renal AKI.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has had 3 days of vomiting after a holiday abroad. He feels weak and dizzy. He has no abdominal pain, no black stools and no previous kidney problems. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his blood results?
practice.e: Raised urea with normal creatinine, high sodium and high haematocrit is the signature of dehydration. A GI bleed raises urea but lowers haemoglobin.

steps.x: Explain the blood pattern.
Urea high, creatinine normal, sodium and haematocrit high: concentrated blood.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dehydration**.

elim: ATN raises creatinine as well; his is normal.
CKD raises creatinine and he has no kidney history.
Rhabdomyolysis raises creatinine and CK, often with dark urine.
A bleed raises urea but lowers haemoglobin, and he has no melaena.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: high urea, normal creatinine, high haematocrit = dehydration.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman is admitted with 4 days of diarrhoea and reduced oral intake. She is dizzy on standing. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. Her mucous membranes are dry.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: U&Es are the first-line test: urea is the most sensitive marker, and sodium, potassium and creatinine guide fluid choice and show AKI.

steps.x: First-line test in a clinically dehydrated patient.
Dehydrated; you need the urea, sodium, potassium and creatinine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: She is not febrile or septic.
No respiratory symptoms.
Ultrasound is for suspected obstruction, not first-line here.
Urine tests are second-line.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: dehydration = clinical diagnosis, then U&Es first.

practice.stem: An 86 year old man is admitted with dehydration after a week of poor intake in hot weather. His serum sodium is 151 mmol/L. His urine is dark and scanty. A urine sample is sent to help confirm that his kidneys are responding normally.
practice.q: Which is the most likely urine finding?
practice.e: In dehydration, ADH and RAAS concentrate the urine: low volume, high osmolality. Dilute urine with high sodium would suggest diabetes insipidus.

steps.x: Most likely urine result in dehydration.
Normal kidneys save water when dry.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Concentrated urine, high osmolality**.

elim: Dilute urine with high sodium means diabetes insipidus.
Glycosuria needs hyperglycaemia.
Heavy proteinuria is glomerular disease.
Red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: dry patient + working kidneys = small volumes of concentrated urine.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has had diarrhoea for 2 days after eating at a barbecue. She feels thirsty and has a dry mouth but is alert and able to drink. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild to moderate dehydration (thirst, dry mouth, normal BP, able to drink) is treated first-line with oral rehydration solution.

steps.x: Initial management: grade severity first.

clues: thirsty and has a dry mouth
steps.x: Normal BP, alert, drinking: mild to moderate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral rehydration solution**.

elim: IV saline is for severe dehydration.
HAS is for severe burns when crystalloid fails.
Loperamide does not replace the fluid deficit.
She is not vomiting; an antiemetic does not rehydrate.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: mild to moderate = ORS first-line.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has had severe vomiting for 3 days and is now confused. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and capillary refill 5 seconds. He has passed no urine for 8 hours.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Severe dehydration with shock needs IV 0.9% saline. 5% glucose does not stay in the circulation; oral and subcutaneous routes are too slow.

steps.x: Initial management in a shocked patient.
Hypotension, confusion, anuria: severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV 0.9% saline** bolus, then reassess.

elim: 5% glucose distributes into all compartments and will not restore BP.
HAS is for severe burns when crystalloid fails.
He is confused and vomiting; oral fluid will not work.
Subcutaneous fluid is far too slow for shock.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: severe = IV 0.9% saline.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has 40% partial-thickness burns from a house fire. He has received crystalloid by the burns formula for 12 hours but remains hypotensive with low urine output. His pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 86/52 mmHg. He has worsening generalised oedema.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: In severe burns where crystalloid alone is not enough, human albumin solution restores intravascular volume and limits excessive oedema.

steps.x: Next step when crystalloid has failed in burns.
Crystalloid alone insufficient, albumin very low, oedema increasing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Human albumin solution**.

elim: 5% glucose leaves the circulation and worsens oedema.
No reason to suspect adrenal crisis.
Oral fluid cannot resuscitate a shocked burns patient.
His haematocrit is high; he is not anaemic.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: severe burns, crystalloid not enough = HAS.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman is admitted with dehydration after 4 days of diarrhoea. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. Her urea has risen much more than her creatinine.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the disproportionate rise in urea?
o: Increased passive reabsorption of urea with water in the proximal tubule
practice.e: Urea is reabsorbed passively with water in the proximal tubule, so it rises more when the kidney saves water. Creatinine is not affected by water reabsorption.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why urea rises more than creatinine.

clues: urea has risen much more than her creatinine
steps.x: Volume depletion makes the kidney reabsorb more water.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urea **follows water passively** in the proximal tubule.

elim: Hepatic urea output rises with protein loads or GI bleeds, not this.
Muscle breakdown raises creatinine and CK.
Less creatinine production would not raise urea.
Creatinine secretion does not explain a high urea.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: urea follows water; creatinine does not.

prompts.q: What is dehydration and what are its common causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: find the route of loss in the stem.

points.p: A deficit of body water, reducing circulating volume and upsetting electrolytes
points.why: Volume loss drives the clinical picture.
Older people with blunted thirst are at risk.
Glucose drags water into the urine.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and signs of dehydration?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'most likely finding' is a sign of dryness, not overload.

prompts.q: Which features separate mild to moderate from severe dehydration?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity decides oral versus IV fluid.

points.p: Mild to moderate: thirst and dry mouth

prompts.q: What is the classic blood picture of dehydration, and what are its complications?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: urea out of proportion to creatinine.

points.p: Disproportionate rise in urea relative to creatinine
points.why: A ratio above about 100 suggests pre-renal.
Concentrated blood; separates it from a GI bleed.
Listed as a complication in the notes.

prompts.q: How do you tell dehydration from diabetes insipidus and from an upper GI bleed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: urine osmolality and haemoglobin decide.

points.p: Diabetes insipidus: large volumes of dilute urine
GI bleed raises urea but haemoglobin falls

prompts.q: How is dehydration diagnosed, and what are the first and second-line tests?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical diagnosis first, then U&Es.

points.p: Clinical assessment is the gold standard
points.why: History and examination make the diagnosis.

points.p: Urea is the most sensitive marker

points.why: Look for diabetes and the high haematocrit.

prompts.q: How do you treat mild to moderate versus severe dehydration?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: grade first, then pick the route.

points.p: Mild to moderate: oral rehydration solution

prompts.q: What else must you do after initial rehydration, and when is human albumin solution used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: slow correction and treat the cause.

points.p: Correct electrolytes carefully, monitoring sodium and potassium
Correct slowly to avoid rapid shifts
points.why: Fast correction of high sodium causes cerebral oedema.

points.p: HAS in severe burns when crystalloid alone is insufficient

prompts.q: Why does the urine become concentrated, and why does urea rise more than creatinine?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two hormones, one passive process.

points.why: Water reabsorbed in the collecting duct.

points.p: Urea is reabsorbed passively with water in the proximal tubule
points.why: Creatinine is not affected by water reabsorption.

prompts.q: Why is severe dehydration dangerous, and why must hypernatraemia be corrected slowly?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: shock now, cerebral oedema later if you rush.

points.p: Hypovolaemic shock when volume falls below what maintains organ perfusion

points.why: Brain cells adapted to hypertonicity take up water too fast.

points.p: Isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic depending on water vs salt loss

glossary.dehydration: A deficit of body water that reduces circulating volume and disturbs electrolytes.
glossary.oliguria: Reduced urine output, usually under 0.5 mL/kg per hour in adults.
glossary.skin turgor: How quickly pinched skin springs back; slow return suggests dehydration.
glossary.mucous membranes: Moist linings such as the inside of the mouth and tongue; dry in dehydration.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure: height of the neck vein pulsation, low when the patient is dry.
glossary.capillary refill: Time for colour to return after pressing the skin; over 2 seconds suggests poor perfusion.
glossary.hypovolaemic shock: Circulatory failure from too little circulating volume to perfuse the organs.
glossary.hypotension: Low blood pressure, usually systolic below 90 mmHg.
glossary.tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.haematocrit: The proportion of blood volume made up of red cells; rises when the blood is concentrated.
glossary.urea: Waste product of protein breakdown; the most sensitive U&E marker of dehydration.
glossary.creatinine: Waste product from muscle, filtered by the kidney and used to estimate kidney function.
glossary.urea:creatinine ratio: Urea divided by creatinine; a high ratio suggests a pre-renal, volume-depleted state.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: the routine kidney blood test (sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine).
glossary.osmolality: The concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid.
glossary.pre-renal AKI: Kidney injury caused by reduced blood flow to the kidneys rather than kidney damage itself.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a rapid fall in kidney function over hours to days.
glossary.SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: too much ADH causing water retention and low sodium.
glossary.ADH: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): makes the kidney reabsorb water in the collecting duct.
glossary.RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: hormones that raise blood pressure and retain sodium and water.
glossary.aldosterone: Adrenal hormone that makes the kidney retain sodium and water and lose potassium.
glossary.aquaporins: Water channels inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
glossary.proximal tubule: First part of the kidney tubule, where most water, sodium and urea are reabsorbed.
glossary.osmotic diuresis: Increased urine output because a solute such as glucose drags water into the urine.
glossary.ORS: Oral rehydration solution: water with set amounts of salt and glucose to aid absorption.
glossary.oral rehydration solution: Water with set amounts of salt and glucose that the gut absorbs efficiently.
glossary.0.9% saline: Isotonic sodium chloride solution; a crystalloid that expands circulating volume.
glossary.crystalloid: A clear IV fluid of salts in water, such as 0.9% saline.
glossary.Human Albumin Solution: Purified human albumin given IV to hold fluid in the circulation, e.g. in severe burns.
glossary.cerebral oedema: Swelling of the brain from excess water, causing drowsiness and seizures.
glossary.osmotic demyelination: Brainstem damage from correcting a low sodium too quickly.
glossary.hypertonic: Having a higher solute concentration than plasma.
glossary.hypotonic: Having a lower solute concentration than plasma.
glossary.isotonic: Having the same solute concentration as plasma.
glossary.diabetes insipidus: Lack of, or resistance to, ADH, causing large volumes of dilute urine.
glossary.norovirus: A highly infectious virus causing outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea, often in care homes.
glossary.ramipril: An ACE inhibitor; can worsen pre-renal AKI when a patient is dehydrated.
glossary.bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic that increases salt and water loss.
